memory_line: Phenytoin: slow, saline, and a monitor.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 1:05 AM. He's 72, 70 kg, with a heart history. His seizure stopped after lorazepam.
• Order: phenytoin 1,400 mg IV (intravenous) loading dose

❌ 3 mistakes
1️⃣ Mixed it in dextrose, no filter
2️⃣ Ran it in 10 minutes
3️⃣ No cardiac monitor, no BP (blood pressure) checks
➡️ BP 72/40, heart rate 38, wide beats. Rapid response.

🧮 The math
• 1,400 mg ÷ 50 mg a minute = 28 minutes, at the fastest
• He got it in 10. That's 140 mg a minute

💉 Phenytoin IV (SLOW AND SALINE)
• Too fast: low BP and dangerous heart rhythms
• Adults: no faster than 50 mg a minute. Older adults or heart disease: slower, as ordered
• Normal saline only. It can form crystals in dextrose
• In-line filter, flush with saline before and after
• Cardiac monitor and BP during and after the infusion
• Watch the IV site: it can burn and damage tissue

📊 Therapeutic level: 10 to 20 mcg/mL (micrograms per milliliter)

🧠 Phenytoin: slow, saline, and a monitor.

rn_checks: Loading dose 20 mg/kg per the AES 2016 status epilepticus guideline (70 kg = 1,400 mg; the label lists 10 to 15 mg/kg); adult max rate 50 mg a minute; label recommends slower rates, complications most common in older and critically ill patients
Boxed warning: hypotension and arrhythmias with rapid IV administration; continuous ECG and BP monitoring during and after
Dilute in normal saline only (precipitates in dextrose); in-line filter; flush with saline before and after
IV site: extravasation and soft tissue injury (purple glove syndrome) risk
Story outcome: BP 72/40, heart rate 38, wide beats after 140 mg a minute in a 72-year-old with heart disease. Realistic?
